statement: In 9 healthy non-smoking men (mean age 24.6) in a Swedish laboratory, each given the same small amount of alcohol (0.30 g per kg of body weight, diluted to 20% in orange juice and drunk within 15 minutes; study conditions) on five occasions at least a week apart in random order (Jones et al., 1997), drinking a few minutes after a breakfast of about 3,000 kJ, compared with drinking after a 10-hour overnight fast, reduced the peak blood alcohol concentration and the area under the blood-alcohol curve over 210 minutes by roughly half: peaks were 16.6, 17.7 and 13.3 mg/dl after breakfasts rich in fat, carbohydrate and protein, against 30.8 mg/dl after fasting (43 to 57 in 100 of the fasting peak; editors' calculation), and the areas 1,767, 1,619 and 1,270 against 3,210 mg/dl·min (40 to 55 in 100); the same dose infused into a vein gave a peak of 54.3 mg/dl. No test of each breakfast against fasting is printed, but by the editors' estimate each difference is several times its standard error. The three breakfasts did not differ significantly, but that comparison had little power (0.22 and 0.25, and the authors call for caution), and the protein-rich breakfast, which also had about 9 in 100 more energy, gave peaks 20 to 25 in 100 lower than the other two (editors' calculation), so the study cannot show whether the kind of food matters. After the fat- and carbohydrate-rich breakfasts the peak came 30 to 90 minutes after drinking (30 to 60 after the protein-rich one and after fasting), and after food it varied more between men (coefficients of variation 24 to 40 in 100, against 14 after fasting). The authors explain the lower values by slower emptying of the stomach letting the liver break down more alcohol before it reaches the blood, or by part of the alcohol being held by the meal; neither was measured, and their statement that alcohol left the blood 1 to 2 hours sooner after food comes from looking at the curves, not from a measurement. The study gave one small amount, to young men only, measured no impairment, and did not test larger amounts, women, other meals or longer gaps between eating and drinking. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: In a small laboratory study, 9 young men drank the same small amount of alcohol on different days. When they had eaten a breakfast just before, the highest level of alcohol in their blood was about half of what it was when they had eaten nothing since the night before (13 to 18 against 31 mg per 100 ml). The kind of breakfast made no clear difference, but the study was too small to tell. Larger amounts, women, other meals and how drunk people felt were not studied.

exposure: Drinking 0.30 g of alcohol per kg (20% v/v in orange juice, finished within 15 minutes) a few minutes after a breakfast of about 2,900 to 3,200 kJ rich in fat, carbohydrate or protein, eaten in 15 minutes (study conditions)
comparator: The same men drinking the same amount after a 10-hour overnight fast; the same dose infused into a vein over 30 minutes
outcome: Venous blood alcohol: peak concentration, time to peak and area under the concentration–time curve from 0 to 210 minutes
magnitude: Jones et al. (1997), n = 9, mean (SD): peak mg/dl, fat-rich 16.6 (4.0), carbohydrate-rich 17.7 (7.1), protein-rich 13.3 (4.0), fasting 30.8 (4.3), intravenous 54.3 (6.4); AUC 0–210 min, mg/dl·min, 1,767 (549), 1,619 (760), 1,270 (406), 3,210 (527), 4,786 (446). Five conditions: F = 98.7 (peak) and 88.9 (AUC), P < 0.001; three meals: F = 2.22 and 2.42, P > 0.05, post hoc power 0.22 and 0.25. Time to peak 30–90 min (fat- and carbohydrate-rich), 30–60 min (protein-rich, fasting), 30 min (intravenous). Coefficients of variation: peak 24–40% after meals, 14% fasting; AUC 31–47% and 16%. Editors' calculations: meal peaks 43–57% and AUCs 40–55% of the fasting values; protein-rich peak about 20% and 25% lower than fat- and carbohydrate-rich, AUC about 28% and 22% lower; each meal–fasting difference about 5 to 9 times its approximate standard error (five-condition residual SD, assuming sphericity).

statement: In adults with panic disorder diagnosed by a clinician and tested in laboratories while off psychiatric medicines, a single oral dose of caffeine of 400 to about 750 mg (480 mg in 7 of 10 studies; study conditions), compared with a placebo of the same or similar taste in the same people, increases the chance of a panic attack within hours, by a meta-analysis of 10 small blinded challenge studies published from 1985 to 2015 (Klevebrant & Frick, 2022): in the 9 studies that reported panic attacks, 121 of 237 people with panic disorder (51 in 100) had one after caffeine, and no study reported one after placebo; in the 6 studies that also tested people without panic disorder, 69 of 128 people with panic disorder (54 in 100) had one after caffeine against 2 of 115 healthy controls (2 in 100), a difference of 52 in 100 (editors' calculation). The paper prints two incompatible pooled risk ratios for that comparison (about 32 by its text and 12.1 in its figure), so the counts are the better summary. Self-rated anxiety rose after caffeine in both groups, more on average in people with panic disorder (standardized difference 1.02, 95% CI 0.09 to 1.96), but the studies varied widely (prediction interval −1.27 to 3.32; about 0.72 without one outlying study, editors' recalculation), and these rises were measured after caffeine without a placebo comparison, which only 2 studies reported. The authors equate 480 mg with about 5 cups of brewed coffee at about 100 mg a cup, so the doses tested correspond to about 4 to 7.5 such cups taken at once (editors' calculation); no study tested less than 400 mg, so what everyday amounts do in panic disorder is not known. All studies were done at rest during a break from psychiatric medicines; 2 always gave caffeine last, and 8 of the 10 come from two research groups. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In small laboratory studies, about half of adults with panic disorder had a panic attack after one large dose of caffeine (121 of 237), and none after a dummy drink or capsule. Among people without panic disorder, 2 of 115 had one. The doses were like 4 or more cups of coffee at once, and smaller amounts were never tested, so what a cup or two does is not known.
population: Adults with panic disorder diagnosed by a clinician (DSM-III to DSM-5 or ICD criteria), mostly recruited from outpatient clinics and tested during a break from psychiatric medicines: 244 people in 10 studies (1985 to 2015), and 122 psychiatrically healthy controls in 7 of the studies
exposure: A single oral dose of caffeine given blind at rest: 480 mg in 7 studies, 400 mg in 1, and 10 or 7 mg per kg in 2 (about 750 and 525 mg at 75 kg), as capsules, instant coffee or other drinks (study conditions)
comparator: Placebo with the same or similar taste in the same people (all studies); healthy controls given the same challenge (7 studies)
outcome: Panic attack within 30 to 240 minutes (self- or clinician-reported); change in self-rated anxiety
magnitude: Klevebrant & Frick (2022): panic attacks after caffeine 121/237 (51.1%) with panic disorder in 9 studies and 2/115 (1.7%) controls; none after placebo in any study. In the 6 studies with both groups 69/128 (53.9%) against 2/115 (1.7%), risk difference 52.2 percentage points (editors' calculation); pooled log RR 3.47 (95% CI 2.06 to 4.87) in the text, which is RR about 32 (7.8 to 130; editors' calculation), against RR 12.12 (6.06 to 24.23) in Fig. 4. Studies without controls: 52/109 (47.7%). Anxiety change after caffeine (6 studies; 121 with panic disorder, 111 controls): g 1.94 (1.19 to 2.69) and 0.91 (0.46 to 1.36); difference g 1.02 (0.09 to 1.96), I² 66.8%, prediction interval −1.27 to 3.32; about 0.72 (0.07 to 1.37) without the outlying study (editors' recalculation). Doses 400 to about 750 mg, about 4 to 7.5 cups of brewed coffee at about 100 mg a cup (editors' calculation from the authors' equivalence of 480 mg with about 5 cups).

statement: In healthy volunteers in laboratory studies, evidence is insufficient to say whether CBD taken with, or shortly before, THC changes THC's effects, compared with the same amount of THC taken the same way without CBD: results differ between studies and outcomes, and no pattern by amount, route or ratio has been found. A systematic review of such studies (Freeman et al., 2019; searched to February 2019; 16 studies in 23 articles published from 1974 to 2019, 13 crossover and 3 parallel-group, 466 healthy volunteers in all, almost all of whom had used cannabis before, mostly occasionally; nothing pooled; the editors rate confidence in the review critically low) covers THC swallowed, injected into a vein, smoked, vaporised or sprayed in the mouth, in widely different amounts and ratios. As summarized there, most studies found no significant difference with CBD in THC's blood levels (most of eight studies; one vaporised study of 14 people found a higher peak with CBD), in the rise in heart rate (no difference in nine of ten studies) or in how intoxicated people felt (seven of nine; two small studies, one smoked and one by mouth, found less). Reports of less anxiety or fewer psychosis-like effects with CBD come mainly from four studies in which THC was swallowed or injected into a vein: groups of 5 given THC by mouth (the most intense grade of effects, such as panic, in 4 of 5 after THC alone against 3 of 15 with CBD added; no statistical test reported in the review), a crossover of 8 people given both by mouth, a pseudo-randomised crossover of 6 people given both into a vein (3 of whom had psychosis-like effects after THC alone), and a parallel trial of 48 people given THC into a vein after CBD or a placebo by mouth, in which the average rise in psychosis-like symptoms did not differ although fewer of those given CBD had a clinically significant rise; the review's discussion nonetheless describes three of these studies as showing significantly fewer people with extreme anxiety or psychosis-like effects. With vaporised THC, a 48-person crossover found no difference in psychosis-like effects, and in the 14-person study anxiety rose 15 minutes after THC with and without CBD and was still raised an hour later only without it. Results on memory, attention and movement tasks went in both directions. In a later randomized, double-blind crossover trial in a laboratory, 18 healthy adults who had used cannabis before but not in the previous 30 days (the completers of 22 randomized; Zamarripa et al., 2023) each ate, in random order on days at least a week apart, a placebo brownie, a brownie with a THC-dominant whole-plant extract (20 mg THC, no CBD) and a brownie with a CBD-dominant extract (20 mg THC with 640 mg CBD), and swallowed a cocktail of five probe medicines, including the sedative midazolam, 30 minutes later in every session (study conditions only). Compared with the THC-dominant brownie, the CBD-dominant brownie was associated with higher blood levels of THC and of 11-OH-THC, a substance the body makes from THC (peaks 14.8 against 8.2 and 53.9 against 4.5, units not printed in the text: about 1.8 and 12 times higher, editors' arithmetic), and with stronger effects, most of them unwanted. Peak rises from each session's baseline on 0–100 scales, rated by the participants in double-blind sessions, were larger for drug effect (72.8 against 59.2), unpleasant (38.6 against 19.6), feeling sick (26.1 against 11.6), memory trouble (37.8 against 27.4) and difficulty with routine tasks (46.7 against 30.3); scores on an arithmetic task and a divided-attention task were worse (P = .049 and .04), and heart rate rose more (by 25.4 against 10.1 beats a minute). Pleasant and liking ratings did not differ significantly, and anxious (23.9 against 13.3), paranoid (23.4 against 12.0) and sleepy (42.6 against 21.0) ratings, though higher than after placebo, did not differ significantly from the THC-dominant brownie. The placebo brownie with the probe medicines changed no effect measure significantly. Effects were followed for 24 hours: the strongest drug effect came later on average (2.9 against 2.1 hours after the probe medicines; not tested statistically) and total THC exposure (area under the curve) was about 2.5 times higher (editors' arithmetic), but how long the stronger effects lasted is not given in the parts of the paper that could be read. In these conditions the CBD-dominant extract did not soften THC's effects, which the authors present as contrary to common claims that CBD dampens THC's unwanted effects; whether the difference came from CBD, from the extract's other cannabinoids or from changed levels of the probe medicines, which the paper does not report, cannot be told, and the trial tested one amount of CBD, eaten in the same brownie as the THC, in adults who had not used cannabis for at least 30 days; smoked or vaped cannabis was not tested. This trial's result differs from most earlier studies, and so do its conditions: a large amount of CBD, eaten in a whole-plant extract, with probe medicines. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Lab studies disagree on whether CBD changes how THC feels. In most of 16 older studies, adding CBD made no clear difference to how high people felt, to their heart rate or to THC in their blood. A few small studies, in which THC was swallowed or injected, found less anxiety or fewer paranoid feelings with CBD; studies with vaporised THC found little or no difference. In one later trial, 18 healthy adults who ate THC with a large amount of CBD had more THC in their blood, felt the drug more, felt sicker and had more trouble with memory and simple tasks, but other test medicines, including a sedative, were also given. No pattern by amount or by way of taking it has been found.
population: Healthy volunteers in laboratory studies: 466 in 16 studies from 1974 to 2019 gathered by one systematic review (all but two studies admitted only people with previous cannabis use, mostly occasional), and, in one later trial, 18 healthy adults aged 18 to 50 (11 men, 7 women; mean age 30) with past cannabis use but none in the 30 days before the first session (mean 124 days since last use), completers among 22 randomized, at the Johns Hopkins Behavioral Pharmacology Research Unit, United States
exposure: CBD given with, or shortly before, the same dose of THC by the same route (swallowed, injected into a vein, smoked, vaporised or sprayed in the mouth, in widely varying amounts and ratios; review studies); in the later trial, a brownie with a CBD-dominant whole-plant extract (20 mg THC with 640 mg CBD; the extract also held about 2% CBC and 1% CBG), followed 30 minutes later by a cocktail of five probe medicines (caffeine, omeprazole, losartan, dextromethorphan, midazolam) (study conditions only)
comparator: The same THC dose by the same route without CBD, or after a placebo pre-treatment, with a placebo condition or a pre-drug baseline (review studies); in the later trial, the same participants after a brownie with a THC-dominant extract carrying the same nominal THC dose (20 mg THC, no detectable CBD) and after a placebo brownie, each with the same probe cocktail
outcome: Blood levels of THC, heart rate, self-rated intoxication, anxiety, psychosis-like symptoms, memory, attention and psychomotor tasks, as each study measured them (review); in the later trial, plasma THC, 11-OH-THC and THC-COOH; peak change from baseline in self-ratings on the Drug Effect Questionnaire (0–100), cognitive task performance and heart rate over 24 hours
magnitude: Freeman et al. (2019), as summarized by the review (no pooled estimates or effect sizes; amounts are study conditions, as printed in its text): pharmacokinetics, mostly no significant change in eight studies; higher peak plasma THC with vaporised THC 13.75 mg plus CBD 13.75 mg than with THC alone (n = 14; area under the curve higher, not significantly); later time to peak THC with an oromucosal spray of THC 10 mg plus CBD 10 mg (n = 24). Pulse: no difference in nine of ten studies (editors' count from the text); differences in both directions in one study with 5 per group. Intoxication: less with CBD in two of nine studies (smoked THC 0.025 mg/kg with CBD 0.150 mg/kg, n = 15; oral THC 0.5 mg/kg with CBD 1 mg/kg, n = 8). Anxiety: grade 4 effects in 4 of 5 after oral THC 30 mg alone against 3 of 15 with oral CBD 15, 30 or 60 mg added (no test reported); a smaller STAI rise after oral THC 0.5 mg/kg with CBD 1 mg/kg (n = 8); vaporised THC 13.75 mg with or without CBD 13.75 mg raised anxiety at 15 minutes, still raised at an hour only without CBD (n = 14). Psychosis-like effects: in 3 of 6 after intravenous THC 1.25 mg, lessened by intravenous CBD 5 mg beforehand (pseudo-randomised crossover); after intravenous THC 1.5 mg, no difference in the mean PANSS rise between oral CBD 600 mg and placebo beforehand, with fewer people showing a rise of at least 3 points in positive symptoms and lower paranoia with CBD (parallel, n = 48); no difference with vaporised THC 8 mg with or without CBD 16 mg (crossover, n = 48). No consistent pattern by route, dose or THC:CBD ratio; the review's own summary of routes and dose ranges disagrees with its Table 1, so no per-route study counts are given here. Zamarripa et al. (2023), CBD-dominant against THC-dominant extract, mean (SD): THC peak 14.8 (5.5) against 8.2 (4.0), area under the curve 84.9 (29.38) against 33.3 (16.9); 11-OH-THC peak 53.9 (22.6) against 4.5 (1.9), area 349.0 (137.1) against 34.0 (16.4); all P < .001; units not printed in the text (editors' arithmetic: THC peak about 1.8 and area about 2.5 times, 11-OH-THC peak about 12 and area about 10 times higher). Peak change from baseline on 0–100 ratings, CBD-dominant against THC-dominant: drug effect 72.8 against 59.2; unpleasant 38.6 against 19.6; sick 26.1 against 11.6; dry or red eyes 28.8 against 15.9; memory 37.8 against 27.4; routine tasks 46.7 against 30.3 (all Tukey P < .05); anxious 23.9 against 13.3, paranoid 23.4 against 12.0, sleepy 42.6 against 21.0 (not significant). Paced serial addition -22.7 against -6.6 correct (P = .049); divided-attention tracking error 32.7 against 15.9 (higher is worse; P = .04); heart rate +25.4 against +10.1 beats a minute (P = .001). Time of peak drug effect 2.9 against 2.1 hours (not tested). Many printed Cohen's d values for the effects do not match the printed means and SDs (some, such as drug effect, memory and routine tasks against the THC-dominant extract, do), and several printed intervals include zero beside P < .05; the d values are not used.

risk_of_bias.note: The review's 16 studies are seen only through a review the editors rate critically low on AMSTAR 2 (card sc_freeman_2019: English-language, peer-reviewed-only search; risk of bias not weighed in its conclusions); its own ratings (10 low, 6 some concerns) include a pseudo-randomised study rated low, and its text and table disagree in several places. The later trial, RoB 2 some concerns (card sc_zamarripa_2023): only completers analysed after 4 of 22 randomized dropped out and were replaced; 36 outcomes without correction; the abstract, text and table disagree on several results, and many printed effect sizes do not match the printed data.

inconsistency.note: Directions differ: most studies found no difference on most outcomes; four small studies with THC swallowed or injected reported less anxiety or fewer psychosis-like effects; one vaporised study found a shorter-lasting rise in anxiety but more divided-attention impairment with CBD; the later oral trial found higher blood THC and stronger, mostly unwanted effects; the review found no pattern by route, dose or ratio that would explain the differences.

indirectness.note: The review's studies are second-hand (METHODS §6.3); all used single doses in screened healthy volunteers, most with occasional use, with laboratory routes, amounts and ratios that rarely match products people use; in the later trial, whole-plant extracts carrying other cannabinoids and a probe cocktail including the sedative midazolam, whose levels are not reported.

imprecision.note: Six of the review's studies had 4 to 8 people per condition and nothing was pooled; the later trial had 18 people, with task differences at P = .049 and .04 and printed intervals that cannot be relied on.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed: the review judged it low because studies reported a mix of significant and non-significant results, which is not a method of detecting it; the later trial was registered (NCT04201197).

grade.reasoning: Randomized within-person and parallel laboratory comparisons start high (METHODS §6.3); the review's studies are seen only second-hand. Down one each for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision, giving very low (the floor). The rise in blood THC and 11-OH-THC in the later trial, on its own, is large, objective and precise and would rate low (high, minus risk of bias and indirectness). Worded as insufficient evidence because neither an effect of CBD on THC's acute effects nor its absence can be shown with precision. Status mixed: 17 studies with inconsistent findings and no adequate explanation of the differences. The review (Freeman et al., 2019) is used only for what each study reported, described by route and size, and not for a general claim that CBD protects against THC's anxiety or psychosis-like effects: its discussion calls three studies' results significant where its own summaries give no test for two and no difference in the average for the third. Not yet read: the primary studies, later randomized studies of THC with and without CBD on the reading list (Arkell et al., 2020; Lawn et al., 2023) and a 2026 meta-analysis of blood THC with CBD (Chester et al.).
